newsitem.title: CANADA: Cornucopia says Zaire copper rights unclear.
newsitem.headline: Cornucopia says Zaire copper rights unclear.

text.p: A consortium led by Vancouver-based Cornucopia Resources Ltd says it is still in the running for Zaire's huge Tenke Fungurume copper-cobalt project.
"Our position has not changed," Cornucopia president Andrew Milligan said in an interview on Monday.
A second Canadian company, Vancouver-based Consolidated Eurocan Ventures Ltd, said last week it had virtually sewn up a deal with the Zaire government giving it rights to Tenke Fungurume.
But Cornucopia said the deal was far from certain.

Cornucopia put together a tentative consortium last spring with metals firms Inco Ltd and Phelps Dodge Corp after Zaire's prime minister, Kengo wa Dondo, invited Cornucopia to submit a proposal for the metals deposit, Milligan said.
The prime minister repeated his invitation in September, he said.

But the invitation was verbal and the consortium wanted to wait until the situation was clarified before submitting a proposal. Inco made its participation conditional on the clarification, Milligan said.
And Cornucopia has a third major base metals producer ready to join the consortium, Milligan said.

But Consolidated Eurocan said it has finalized arrangements for a joint venture with Gecamines, Zaire's state-owned mining company and expects the whole deal will be completed by the end of the month.
The deal still requires cabinet approval however, said Milligan.
"Perhaps it's only in our eyes, but we have no positive news one way or the other," he said.
The cabinet could choose to close a deal with Eurocan, consider Cornucopia or reopen the project for worldwide tender, he said.
He expected a decision to be made this week. A spokeswoman for Eurocan also expected final approval soon.

The potential for Tenke Fungurume is enormous. The deposit contains at least 222 million tonnes of resource grading 4.42 percent copper and 0.33 percent cobalt, making it one of the world's largest unexplored copper-cobalt deposits.
The project was previously explored by a consortium led by Anglo American Corp of South Africa, which invested almost US$300 million in the porject but walked away because of political risk.

Milligan estimated it would cost about US$300 million for initial development of Tenke Fungurume, and up to US$3 billion in total capital costs. -- Heather Scoffield, Reuters Toronto Bureau 416 941-8104
